body.text: Former Philippines president Rodrigo Duterte in the chamber of the International Criminal Court during hearings in September (ICC-CPI)
Washington’s double standard in the Philippines
The US can help the Philippines resist Beijing without treating justice for Filipinos as somebody else’s problem.

The two decisions sit uneasily together. Washington is helping Manila defend its rights at sea while penalising a court that Filipino families have spent years trying to reach. Former Philippines president Rodrigo Duterte is presently held at The Hague, after the Philippines government surrendered him to the ICC last year to face charges on human rights abuses during his so-called “war on drugs”.

Philippine coast guard crews facing Chinese pressure are defending Philippine rights, not doing Washington’s bidding. Under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, the allies have expanded US access from five Philippine military sites to nine. In July, Washington joined Manila, Canberra and others in reaffirming that the 2016 South China Sea arbitral award is binding on China and the Philippines. The allies were right to make the point. For Manila, the award is a way to defend its rights without having to match China ship for ship.

The US should enforce its existing restrictions on assistance to security-force units where US authorities have credible information that those units committed gross human rights violations, while continuing to help the Philippines defend its waters.

The arbitral tribunal and the ICC have different mandates. Washington does not have to accept every ruling by an international court to defend the maritime award. The Trump administration says it is protecting Americans from prosecution. But it has gone beyond challenging the ICC’s jurisdiction over US nationals by sanctioning the institution itself. The Treasury has authorised some transactions under exceptions, but the designation is not confined to cases Washington objects to. It applies to the court hearing the Philippine drug-war case.
Opening of charges in the Duterte case at the ICC (ICC-CPI)

Duterte’s trial is scheduled to open on 30 November. It concerns three counts of crimes against humanity involving alleged murder and attempted murder. Whatever the judges decide, those charges cover only a fraction of the deaths associated with the campaign. The Philippine government alone counted 6,252 deaths in official anti-drug operations from July 2016 to May 2022. For most of those deaths, the prospect of an investigation rests with Philippine institutions.

There is a practical place to start. On 9 November, the Philippine Truth Commission, an independent civil society initiative, asked the country’s professional regulator to investigate discrepancies in 13 death certificates. It also wanted the regulator to preserve the records and examine the medical basis for what was recorded. That request does not settle how anyone died or who was responsible. It shows why access to records and independent forensic work matter, whatever happens in The Hague.

Washington should lift the sanctions on the court and put domestic accountability on the agenda of its security talks with Manila. Congress has already required the State Department to assess the human rights record of the Philippine police and armed forces. It should ask the department to report publicly on whether records are being preserved and whether families can find out what happened to cases referred for investigation, without exposing witnesses.

The US should enforce its existing restrictions on assistance to security-force units where US authorities have credible information that those units committed gross human rights violations, while continuing to help the Philippines defend its waters. It can also fund independent forensic work, legal support and witness protection on terms set by Philippine organisations doing the work. Neither step requires Washington to tell a Philippine prosecutor whom to charge.

Manila has every reason to seek strong partners. It also has every reason to ask whether those partners value the country for more than where it sits on the map. Washington can give a better answer without waiting for a verdict in The Hague.
